item.title: Sympathy for a Dog in San Diego Who Seemed to Greet an Intruder
item.description:
So much for guarding the castle.

When an intruder broke into Dante Rowley’s home in San Diego this month, home-security cameras captured his golden retriever, Nash, hiding and panting under the dining room table. The dog stayed there as the man helped himself to yogurt and lay down on a blanket.

Then Nash made his move: he approached the man as he walked near the door, and looked up at him, with his tail wagging and a plush toy in his mouth.

Why didn’t he bark? Was he eager to play?

Where many viewers of the video saw a dog trying to have fun when he should be growling, animal behavior experts offered their own interpretations. Some embraced the idea that Nash was eager to make friends, and others said the dog’s behavior was a sign of an anxious animal.

Dr. Katherine A. Houpt, a professor emeritus at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, thinks Nash is a rather affable retriever.

“The dog wanted someone to play with, and the burglar is as good as anyone,” she said. “It’s a breed that’s often friendly and, apparently, the owners made sure he was socialized with people. So he doesn’t think something awful is going to come in the door, but something fun, a playmate.”

Dr. Carlo Siracusa, a professor of clinical small animal behavior and welfare at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine, had a different view. Hiding, panting and holding a chew toy can all be signs that a dog is stressed, he said. Even a wagging tail can be a sign of increased alertness and emotional arousal. Nash, he said, might simply have approached the man because he was near the door, and the dog wanted to get out.

Dr. Siracusa pointed out that Nash also approached the police with a chew toy in his mouth and scurried outside when they came through the door, holding guns.

“It’s very difficult to understand exactly what the dog had in mind, but I don’t see any evidence the dog is trying to be friendly with the intruder or the police,” Dr. Siracusa said. “This is a human interpretation. It’s not an objective reading of the body language.”

In general, he said, a dog’s response to an intruder comes down to “individual variability,” and, to a lesser extent, their breed. Some may feel sharp fear and respond aggressively, he said, just as some humans might startle more than others when they hear an unfamiliar noise in the night.

Mr. Rowley and his fiancée, Stephanie Calderon, had been preparing to fly home from Chicago on Sept. 5 when his security camera sent him an alert. Someone was breaking into his house. The cameras recorded the man using a ladder to climb through a second-story window and then wander around, with his shirt and shoes off.

Mr. Rowley called the San Diego police, who arrived within minutes, sent a drone inside the house and then arrested the man. He was charged with burglary, vandalism, battery on an officer and drug possession, the police said.

Mr. Rowley said that Nash was unharmed, as was his other dog, Ollie, a longhaired dachshund that had run into the backyard. (Mr. Rowley’s brother, who lives down the street, had been dog sitting.)

“Honestly, Nash is just friendly; he’s not a guard dog by any means, so when I saw his reaction, I was surprised that he wasn’t more excited,” Mr. Rowley said on Friday. “Usually, when he sees new people, he runs over and jumps all over them and is just on them 24-7.”

Marc Bekoff, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and the author of “Dogs Demystified: An A-Z Guide to All Things Canine,” said that a dog’s breed doesn’t determine whether it’s going to be a good guard dog.

“You could train a beagle to be a guard dog,” he said. “To me, it just comes down — like with humans — to early rearing.”

Dr. Bekoff said he wasn’t surprised that Nash greeted the intruder with a toy in his mouth. He said he has a part-Doberman mutt who would have done the same thing.

“I see a total love-muffin,” he said. “What I see is a healthy, socialized dog. He just want to play.”

Dr. Houpt agreed.

“It’s a friendly dog, and the dog doesn’t do a background check before he interacts with people,” she said. “So we need more Nashes, is what I’m trying to say.”

item.title: Trump Has Tried to Ban Reporters From Government Spaces Before
item.description:
The Trump administration has repeatedly moved to ban reporters from the White House and other government property.

In January 2025, Mr. Trump tried to bar Associated Press journalists from parts of the White House, including the Oval Office and Air Force One. The A.P. has sued to restore its access, but that case remains in litigation; in the meantime, A.P. photographers have had continued access to the Oval Office. Its print journalists have had more limited access.

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has also placed limits on reporters’ access to the Pentagon, including a requirement that all journalists be accompanied by an official escort while in the building. The Pentagon also closed the work space used for years by journalists with credentials to cover the military. The New York Times sued over the restrictions, and the litigation continues.

During his first term, Mr. Trump revoked a White House pass for Jim Acosta, the former CNN journalist. CNN succeeded in restoring Mr. Acosta’s press credentials in court.

Mr. Trump also tried to temporarily suspend the press pass of a reporter who traded caustic comments with Sebastian Gorka, a right-wing commentator who worked briefly in the White House. The reporter successfully sued to restore his credential.

item.title: Appeals Court Restricts Trump Administration Deportation Effort
item.description:
The Trump administration will face new requirements before it is allowed to deport people to countries other than their nation of origin, an appeals court ruled on Friday.

The ruling, by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, requires that immigrants facing deportation to so-called third countries be given more due process beforehand — “a meaningful opportunity” to raise fears of persecution or torture. In a 55-page opinion with no dissent, a three-judge panel from the court rejected arguments from the Trump administration that it receives “assurances” from foreign governments that deportees will not be persecuted or tortured and that such communications should be sufficient.

The administration’s current policy “conflicts” with laws and regulations that protect detainees from torture, the judges ruled, and added that they were rejecting an attempt by the Homeland Security Department to carve out an exception to those rules “from whole cloth.”

If the ruling remains in place, it will impose a substantial and time-consuming hurdle on Mr. Trump’s third-country deportation program. The practice of sending deportees to faraway and sometimes dangerous countries, often with just a few hours’ notice, has been one of the administration’s highest-profile attempts to create uncertainty for immigrants already in the United States.

The administration has sent migrants to nations including South Sudan, Liberia and Equatorial Guinea as part of the program. In interviews with The New York Times, some migrants deported to third countries have made harrowing allegations that they were abused by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. The Homeland Security Department has said detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” while in ICE custody, and denied that anyone has been beaten or tortured.

In March, the appeals panel temporarily blocked a ruling by Judge Brian E. Murphy of Massachusetts imposing the new requirements. Friday’s order lifts that block, putting most of the new legal hurdles to third-country deportations into place.

The administration can now appeal the ruling to a larger First Circuit panel or to the Supreme Court.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The case already reached the Supreme Court last year, when the justices agreed to allow eight men who had been sent to Djibouti in violation of a preliminary order from Judge Murphy to be sent onward to South Sudan. That ruling dealt with the issue on a temporary basis, while litigation over it moved forward.

The appeals court on Friday struck down one of the requirements that Judge Murphy had attempted to impose on D.H.S. Judge Murphy would have required the department to prioritize deportees’ home countries as destinations, but the appeals court said that could not be legally mandated.

In a statement, Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the migrants who brought the lawsuit, called Friday’s ruling “a major victory for the basic principle that the government cannot deport people to an unknown country without first telling them where they are being sent and giving them a meaningful opportunity to explain why they would face persecution or torture there.”

The unanimous opinion was written by Judge Seth R. Aframe, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Also on the panel were Judge Jeffrey R. Howard, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, and Judge Lara E. Montecalvo, another appointee of Mr. Biden. Judge Murphy is also a Biden appointee.

item.title: Kennedy Center Supporters Rally Amid Speculation About Possible Demolition
item.description:
A large group of demonstrators locked arms to form a human chain around the Kennedy Center on Friday evening to protest President Trump’s efforts to close and remake the center in his image, amid speculation about a possible effort to demolish the building.

Hundreds of demonstrators, many of them performing artists and workers at the Kennedy Center, sang and played music as they circled the building and the sun set over the embattled cultural institution.

Late Wednesday night, photojournalists captured a series of images through the windows of Air Force One that showed Mr. Trump reviewing a large poster board with what looked like a rendering of a construction site beneath the title: “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

The photos, which circulated online ahead of the rally, appeared to spur turnout. Several demonstrators said they had seen the images but dismissed the possibility of a demolition as another one of Mr. Trump’s publicity stunts. Organizers celebrated a previous court victory removing Mr. Trump’s name from the center and said they hoped that the center would soon reopen, after the board, led by Mr. Trump, moved to close it earlier this week.

“It seems pretty performative,” said David Novy, 51, who attended the rally and has been coming to performances at the Kennedy Center since he was in high school in the 1990s, and is a subscriber to the center’s ballet performances, the Washington National Opera and the National Symphony Orchestra. Those groups have scattered their performances to other venues in the Washington area during the Kennedy Center’s temporary shutdown.

The images of the apparent demolition plan have been incorporated into a previously filed lawsuit over the fate of the Kennedy Center, which after a disastrous year and a half under Mr. Trump’s stewardship, has had plummeting ticket sales and a talent exodus. The center was closed temporarily this week over significant safety concerns, center officials said, after a large chunk of plaster fell from the ceiling.

The crowd, pressed up against security barriers surrounding the center, enveloped the concrete pavilion in front of it, spilled out across 25th Street and onto an adjacent grass lawn. One woman was forcibly escorted away from the building by security guards wearing hard hats after defying the safety perimeter.

Many of the artists at the protest had previously performed at the Kennedy Center, including the Gay Men’s Chorus of Washington, D.C., which had a planned concert canceled last year amid Mr. Trump’s efforts to reshape the institution’s programming. Other performers, like the Rapid Response Choir, have been fixtures of Washington-area protests since Mr. Trump returned to office last year.

Lynda Carter, the actress who played Wonder Woman, and local officials, including Robert White, an at-large member of the District of Columbia Council, attended and spoke at the rally.

“There is no way, no how,” Mr. White said, “that while I am standing, and while you people are standing, that he is going to take this building or take this city. So I plan that I will keep fighting, I will keep screaming, and I will throw some punches if need be.” The crowd cheered.

In an interview, Mr. White said he thought that Mr. Trump was lashing out after a federal judge ordered his administration to remove his name from the center — which was named by Congress to honor President John F. Kennedy after his assassination.

“Anything that he can’t have and try to steal, he wants to destroy,” Mr. White said. “But it is important that we not let him do that.”

Organizers had previously held demonstrations against Mr. Trump’s takeover of the Kennedy Center, but the turnout on Friday night was the largest in support of the performing arts institution. Tara Hoot, a drag queen performer and organizer of the demonstrations in support of the Kennedy Center, noted that a typical protest would draw between 60 and 100 people.

item.title: A Texas Ghost Town Faces an Unlikely Second Act
item.description:
In its heyday, the silver mining town of Shafter, Texas, tucked away along the Eastern edge of the Chinati Mountains, drew hundreds of workers, some from as far away as California. A couple of saloons, a dance hall, a post office and a schoolhouse were built to accommodate its growing population. The Presidio Mine would ultimately produce more than 90 percent of the silver mined in Texas.

By 1942, the quality of the ore had declined, reserves had dwindled and water flooded the mine’s lower levels. A wartime shortage of miners added to the problems, and the mine closed that year. A few years later, most of the people were gone.

Today, about two dozen people live in Shafter, 20 miles north of the Rio Grande, among adobe walls receding back into the ground they came from. For those who remain, the isolation is part of the appeal.

Over Labor Day weekend, some 200 visitors disrupted that quiet. There were local officials, two state legislators, one of Houston’s most prominent defense lawyers and a delegation from Ojinaga, across the river in Mexico. All of them came at the invitation of John Poindexter, an 81-year-old billionaire who owns about a fifth of the town’s center and intends to bring Shafter back to life.

Mr. Poindexter often votes Republican and takes a hard line on illegal immigration. He also opposes the federal border construction in Big Bend National Park and an Australian company’s plan to restart the Shafter mine, and he said he was having trouble accepting Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, as a viable nominee.

Plenty of people in Far West Texas hold some version of those contradictions. Few own as much as Mr. Poindexter does. In Texas, where about 95 percent of land is privately held, according to researchers at Texas A&M, what survives often depends less on public policy than on people like him.

“I’ve never been married, I have no children,” Mr. Poindexter said at Cibolo Creek Ranch, the luxury ranch hotel he owns in West Texas, explaining why no family will inherit what he’s built.

The Tidewater and Big Bend Foundation, a nonprofit Mr. Poindexter funds himself, will eventually own all his properties, including the 30,000-acre ranch, where Justice Antonin Scalia died while on a hunting trip at the ranch in 2016, and additional properties in Tidewater, Virginia. Through it, he plans to turn Shafter into a living history museum and resort, with a restored saloon, post office and general store, along with a dozen adobe residences that will be available to rent.

“I think that we’ve forgotten our origins,” Mr. Poindexter said of the project, which he sees as largely educational. “We’ve forgotten this enormous debt we have to prior generations.”

But Mr. Poindexter is not the only one with plans for this part of Texas.

Federal contractors began clearing ground for a patrol road and vehicle barriers in Big Bend National Park, roughly 60 miles southeast, under the waiver of environmental law and over the objections of local law enforcement. The work is paused until at least Sept. 30 to allow for more public input. Black Bear Minerals, an Australian company, is preparing to restart the Shafter mine, which last operated in 2013.

Wearing his trademark banded collar, a style of shirt he had custom-designed in Merida, Mexico, Mr. Poindexter shook hands with guests as they arrived in Shafter. They were handed maps for a self-guided tour, along with fliers describing opposition to the mine.

Inside one of his homes, Alicia Warlick, Mr. Poindexter’s former fiancée, whom he described as a “close friend,” gave a tour of the house, which she designed. A gallery wall in the foyer traced the history of Shafter’s mining operations through framed photographs and artifacts, while the broad expanses of glass in the living room offered views of the surrounding town.

Above a large wooden dining table hung an equally imposing American Western painting of an eager-looking pioneer woman standing over what appeared to be a dead cow.

“I think John chose that, but I certainly appreciate it,” Ms. Warlick said.

Mr. Poindexter is a Houston native who made his money later in life. He volunteered for the Army out of college and served in the Vietnam War. He received two Silver Stars and two Purple Hearts, then spent 14 years in finance. He founded J.B. Poindexter & Co. in 1985, at 41, and still owns all of it. The company owns a collection of manufacturers, including Morgan Olson, which builds commercial truck bodies and the familiar brown delivery vans used by UPS. J.B. Poindexter & Co. reports about $2.5 billion in annual revenue. Mr. Poindexter keeps a miniature UPS truck at his ranch.

In a grassy clearing, the crowd of bobbing cowboy hats settled into white chairs arranged around tables. Among Mr. Poindexter’s guests were former Mayor Ron Nirenberg of San Antonio; State Senator Roland Gutierrez, a Democrat who represents a vast stretch of the border region; and State Representative Eddie Morales, also a Democrat. Several representatives from Ojinaga, the Mexican city across the border, were also in attendance.

“This has always been a cross-border community,” said Mr. Poindexter, though he said he had not traveled across the border in years. “My insurers are not enthusiastic about my running any kidnapping risk.”

As several of those guests took to the podium, they spoke to the future of the region, and the preservation of its heritage. The prospect of border wall construction in the Big Bend lingered over the speeches.

“It’s obscene,” Mr. Poindexter said of a recent video depicting bulldozers running through Big Bend National Park’s Santa Elena Canyon.

Also present was Dick DeGuerin, a prominent Houston criminal defense attorney who has represented a number of high-profile clients, including David Koresh, the Branch Davidian leader at the center of the 1993 Waco siege, and Robert Durst, the New York real estate heir who was convicted of murder. In 2023, he and Rusty Hardin served as impeachment prosecutors in the trial of Mr. Paxton, who was acquitted.

More recently, Mr. DeGuerin and Mr. Gutierrez have represented a Lipan Apache preservation group and an outdoor recreation company in a federal lawsuit challenging the construction in the Big Bend region.

Mr. DeGuerin has known Mr. Poindexter since the early days of Cibolo Creek Ranch. To celebrate the ranch’s opening in 1995, Mr. Poindexter organized a cattle drive from Marfa to Cibolo Creek, a 30-mile journey that included a herd of 100 longhorns. It took five days.

“We slept on the ground at night in tepees,” said Mr. DeGuerin. “We had a chuck wagon follow us, and we ate off the chuck wagon.”

Decades later, the two men remain close. Mr. DeGuerin was recently admitted to the International Order of St. Hubertus, a centuries-old hunting order complete with elaborate ceremonies and ritualistic robes. Mr. Poindexter is also a member, and Mr. DeGuerin credited him with helping secure his admission.

Their politics have not always aligned. But these days, Mr. Poindexter’s brand of cowboy conservatism does not fit as comfortably within hard-line Texas Republican politics as it once might have.

“I generally vote conservatively, but I’m having great difficulty accommodating myself to what I know of Mr. Paxton’s background,” he said of the coming Senate race.

After the speeches came the customary barbecue. Mr. Poindexter tied on a black apron imprinted with his name and took his place behind a tub of beans, serving guests one by one as they made their way down the line. His white hair waved in the evening breeze, the scene evoking an earlier West.

item.title: Trump Won Their Votes. Now His Trade War Is Dividing Them.
item.description:
President Trump’s decision to escalate a trade war with Canada is threatening to hurt Republicans in the midterm elections, with several Senate battleground states on the northern border feeling an outsize impact.

Many voters say they are upset about the trade war, including some who cast ballots for Mr. Trump in 2024 with hopes that he would bring them relief from rising prices, according to more than four dozen interviews across six states at the center of the battle for control of the Senate.

The intensifying trade conflict — touching steel, dairy, appliances, automotive parts and agricultural equipment — has forced some Republicans to play defense. Democrats have highlighted the costs of the trade fight, which has spooked financial markets and threatened to accelerate inflation driven by Mr. Trump’s unpopular war with Iran.

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican, has pushed Mr. Trump to de-escalate the trade war. In Michigan, the Republican nominee for Senate, Mike Rogers, has appeared to stand uneasily with Mr. Trump’s trade policy.

Nationwide, 78 percent of likely midterm voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 still supported his trade policies, but 19 percent oppose them, according to the latest poll from The New York Times and Siena University. The poll did not ask voters specifically about the trade war with Canada.

The impact of the trade war is felt acutely in states that are along the northern border or have heavily industrial and agricultural economies that make them reliant on trade with Canada — characteristics shared by some of the most competitive Senate battlegrounds.

In interviews in Alaska, Minnesota, Michigan, Maine, New Hampshire and Ohio, many voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 said they believed the president was leveling the playing field with his trade war. But others said the fight with an ally was a mistake.

Candace Oxley, 80, of Kettering, Ohio. Ms. Oxley, a retiree, said that she was dismayed by the trade conflict and that Mr. Trump was preoccupied by vanity projects. His fight with Canada, she said, is not helping Americans afford groceries or gas. “I voted for him, and I wish I had not,” Ms. Oxley said. She said she was unsure how she would vote in Ohio’s competitive Senate race between Jon Husted, the Republican incumbent, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat.

Shkelqim Doko, 65, of Sterling Heights, Mich. Mr. Doko, a bakery owner, said he supported Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada, arguing that the president was working to get even with countries that have taken advantage of the United States. “I stand by my vote,” Mr. Doko said of his support for Mr. Trump in 2024, adding that he sees Mr. Trump as “pro-America.” Mr. Doko said he would vote for Mr. Rogers, the Republican nominee in Michigan’s high-stakes Senate race, because Mr. Rogers would support Mr. Trump’s trade policies. “If we trade,” Mr. Doko said, “we trade in balance.”

Elaine Flowers, 75, of Sterling Heights, Mich. Ms. Flowers, a retired social worker and onetime police officer, expressed hope that the trade war would have long-term benefits. “I just don’t see a good life for my grandkids if we don’t get the industries back in the United States,” Ms. Flowers said. A former Democrat, Ms. Flowers said she now identified as an independent. She said Mr. Trump was the first Republican she voted for after leaving the Democratic Party. She plans to vote for Mr. Rogers in the Senate race in Michigan, she said.

Ben Rackliff, 53, of Jefferson, Maine. Mr. Rackliff, a contractor, said he opposed the trade war and that it had affected his business. “It’s not the presidency I voted for,” said Mr. Rackliff, adding that the president was taking his tariffs “to an extreme.” Still, Mr. Rackliff said he planned to vote for Ms. Collins, a moderate Republican, over the Democratic nominee, Troy Jackson, a former State Senate president. “Whether she’s a RINO or whatever they want to call her, she is present, she does go to the votes,” Mr. Rackliff, using an acronym for Republican in name only, said of Ms. Collins. “She does, for the most part, represent Maine.”

Jonathon Stevens, 24, of Grafton, N.H. Mr. Stevens, a carpenter, said he had voted for Mr. Trump because of his tax policies and what he believed was Mr. Trump’s “blue-collar” approach. But Mr. Stevens said that he was dismayed by Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada, and that he missed former President Barack Obama’s “professionalism.” The United States and Canada are “too close” to be on bad terms, said Mr. Stevens, who considers himself a political independent. He is uncertain who he will vote for in the midterms, he said, but he is leaning toward supporting Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, in the Senate race in New Hampshire.

Stephen Tolan, 63, of Anchorage. Mr. Tolan, a surveyor, said that while the trade war had costs, he ultimately felt Mr. Trump had to ratchet up the tariffs on Canada. “I believe Canada’s been overcharging us for years,” Mr. Tolan said. He added: “Canada’s been living under our umbrella for 250 years. They need to pay up.” Mr. Tolan said he was supporting Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska because the incumbent “backs up Trump.” Mr. Sullivan faces a stiff midterm challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat.

Bennett Coughlan, 34, of Mankato, Minn. Mr. Coughlan, who owns a coffee shop, said that he was generally skeptical of government interference in trade, but that he could accept the use of tariffs with a “clear objective and a way to get back to a stable trading relationship.” The trade war with Canada does not seem to fit that description, he said. “You need some confidence that the rules won’t change overnight,” Mr. Coughlan said, questioning whether the United States should “alienate our allies.” Still, Mr. Coughlan said he did not regret voting for Mr. Trump in 2024, suggesting he did not have a good alternative. And he said he was unsure how he would vote in the Senate race in Minnesota, which pits Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, against the former N.F.L. sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, a Republican.

Kevin Williams in Ohio, Olivia Gieger in New Hampshire, Julia O’Malley in Alaska, Robb Murray in Minnesota and Murray Carpenter in Maine contributed reporting.

item.title: In Redrawn District, a Democrat in North Carolina Trumpets His Centrist Record
item.description:
On the barrier island of Hatteras about 30 miles off the coast of North Carolina, Representative Don Davis approached a group of voters who knew little about him.

The two-term Democrat shook hands and bumped fists with residents seated on folding chairs in a recreation center in the conservative-leaning and predominantly white town of Buxton. Part of the Outer Banks, it was recently swept into his heavily Black district in an aggressive mid-decade redistricting push orchestrated by President Trump ahead of the November midterm elections.

He was there at a meet-and-greet event to ask for their votes, and to persuade them that if he won his race — one critical to his party’s chances of taking control of the House — Congress would not veer too far to the left.

“If things swing, you still have President Trump that’s in the White House,” Mr. Davis said in an interview, after an islander asked him what would happen in the event of a Democratic takeover. “That means you still have to get a signature or be prepared for a veto override.”

It’s a message aimed at countering that of his Republican opponent, Laurie Buckhout, who has portrayed Mr. Davis as a partisan Democrat working in lock step with his party to thwart Mr. Trump’s agenda at every turn.

“Don Davis and the Democrats clearly have a playbook in Washington: Block it in D.C. and then take credit for it back home,” she told a cheering crowd this month at Mr. Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas, where she described Mr. Davis in Trump-like fashion as “Do-Nothing Don.”

Mr. Davis has cultivated a centrist voting record on Capitol Hill, often breaking with his party on key issues. That includes the first legislation Mr. Trump signed in his second term, requiring that immigrants in the country illegally who are accused of crimes be detained for possible deportation. He also bucked Democrats and joined Republicans in voting to end the last year’s government shutdown; criminalize gender-affirming care for minors; and fund ICE without any limits on Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“I take tough votes, I try to do my darnedest,” he told the voters in Buxton. “And I never run away from a vote I take.”

But the race in the newly redrawn district has put Mr. Davis’s cross-party appeal to a steep test.

Last year, state lawmakers approved a new House map that wove ruby-red communities like Buxton, of North Carolina’s Dare County, into the First Congressional District in the heart of the state’s Black Belt.

It also siphoned some of the area’s predominantly Black communities, including in Snow Hill, N.C., the hometown of Mr. Davis, who is Black, into a neighboring district. The new map is one of many in the South that split districts with a sizable share of Black voters.

The new lines have imperiled Mr. Davis’s bid in an already competitive environment. An Air Force veteran and Presbyterian lay minister known to break with his party, Mr. Davis won his race in 2024 against Ms. Buckhout, a white retired Army colonel who served in combat, with just 49.5 percent of the vote, while Mr. Trump won the area with 51 percent. Now he is again facing Ms. Buckhout in a reshaped district that Mr. Trump would have won by nearly 12 points if the same lines had existed two years ago.

It’s the kind of margin that could put Republicans in reach of representing Eastern North Carolina for the first time since 1883.

Political prognosticators regard the district, which has been represented by a Black Democrat since 1992, as either Republican-leaning or a tossup.

Kalshi, the app that allows people to gamble on nearly everything, including U.S. elections, suspended Ms. Buckhout’s account last month after she bet less than $1,000 on her own chances to win, a move that she later said in a statement was “a dumb mistake.”

Ms. Buckhout, who briefly worked in the Trump administration last year as the acting assistant secretary of defense for cyber policy, has worked to portray Mr. Davis as a loyal Democrat, noting that he voted with every member of his party last year against Republicans’ tax and spending domestic policy bill, which extended tax cuts and slashed safety net programs including health care subsidies.

“They did not just vote against the bill; they voted against your paycheck,” Ms. Buckhout said in Texas.

Mr. Davis defended his position, saying he supported the tax cuts, but not at the expense of health care.

“That’s why even a Senator Tom Tillis would vote against” the bill, Mr. Davis said of the outgoing North Carolina Republican, who was one of only three in his party to join Democrats in opposing it.

On the campaign trail, Mr. Davis, an Eastern North Carolina native who grew up cropping tobacco, sought to distance himself from the dysfunction on Capitol Hill, focusing instead on local issues on the coast.

He vowed to deliver for them by working to secure funding for their low-lying two-lane highway with a history of being swallowed by floodwaters and sand during natural disasters.

He played down the national gerrymandering battle that has repeatedly sliced and diced his district, using gallows humor as he acknowledged how difficult it has made for him to campaign for re-election.

“I don’t know how else you draw the district anymore — take it out into the ocean?” he told voters at the rec center, drawing chuckles. “And then I’m going to have to go swim and talk to the fish.”

In an interview, Mr. Davis also rebuffed nearly all questions that weren’t about Eastern North Carolina. He avoided discussing the tensions in his party between centrists like him and democratic socialists, saying that he would work with anybody. He deflected when asked about voters’ frustration with Democrats and Republicans in Washington.

“People are just sick and tired of all this,” he said. “They see everybody’s talking about each other, the attacks, and they’re not talking about them and their issues.”

And he declined to weigh in on whether he would back Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader who is in line to become the first Black speaker should his party win the majority, for the leadership role.

“I’m not making any presumptions that we’re going to win,” he said. “I’m working hard every single day to earn every single vote — and that’s where my focus is; it’s not on what happens when everybody gets sworn in.”

Michael Liberi, a Republican at the meet-and-greet, said he appreciated Mr. Davis’s middle-of-the-road approach and would be backing him.

“I like Don Davis’s energy,” Mr. Liberi, a 64-year-old retiree living in Hatteras, said. “He just hits it on the head when he talks about Eastern North Carolina, and I like his position on working together.”

It has been a matter of political survival for Mr. Davis. In 2024, he was one of five House Democrats who backed the SAVE Act, a bill pushed by Mr. Trump requiring voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote. Mr. Davis has since opposed recent beefed-up versions of the bill, changing his stance after local election officials raised concerns on putting into place such requirements.

More recently, in July, he was one of just a half-dozen Democrats to join Republicans in support of a $1.15 trillion defense policy bill that his party opposed out of fears it would empower Mr. Trump in waging war against Iran. Mr. Davis also voted in September for a Republican resolution condemning socialism, which the vast majority of Democrats opposed, calling it a stunt designed to make their party look extreme.

“I don’t support socialism,” Mr. Davis said in the interview. “OK, let’s now talk about people, families that are hurting here in Eastern North Carolina.”

On Hatteras Island, voters backing Mr. Davis said they were initially concerned that the redrawing of the district would make it impossible for him to win, but had grown more hopeful.

“Everything has gone to hell, period,” Gray Parsons, an independent from Frisco, said. “Redistricting is a part of that.”

Jan Dawson, a Democrat from Buxton, said she had attended the meet and greet to help shore up support for him in her conservative town.

“I suppose the pendulum can swing both ways,” she said of the race. “It’s going to be hard, but not impossible.”

item.title: Tracking Assault Weapons Bans Across the Country
item.description:
State by state, gun rights groups have sought to chip away at bans on assault weapons.

This summer, New Jersey had longstanding limits, among the toughest in the country, tossed out after a federal appeals court ruled them unconstitutional.

The decision, which is paused for now, illustrated the emerging fight over the bans, months before the Supreme Court will consider whether state and local restrictions on the weapons violate the Constitution. It also demonstrated how, more than two decades after the federal assault weapons ban expired, the battle over gun control has moved solidly to states and localities.

The Supreme Court issued a landmark ruling in 2022 that effectively upended gun regulations across the country by establishing a new test for how courts should evaluate laws restricting firearms. Gun rights groups saw an opening to challenge more rules at the state and local level, including assault weapons bans.

Bans on assault weapons are only one category of gun regulation being challenged across the country. But the most immediate consequences would fall on the states that have already sought to limit access to some of the most lethal firearms.

Here’s a closer look at how states regulate assault weapons and how those rules are at stake.

Twelve states and the District of Columbia have passed prohibitions on the sale of assault weapons. Most often, the laws are aimed at restricting semiautomatic rifles that can fire quickly, like an AR-15, but they can also ban handguns and shotguns. Depending on the law, an assault weapon is defined by its model name or a series of features borrowed from guns used in the military. The features include pistol grips, detachable magazines, flash suppressors and folding or collapsible stocks.

In some states, restrictions are already teetering. A federal appeals court ruled to invalidate New Jersey’s law, though it remains in effect until the Supreme Court rules. The decision by the appeals court would appear to threaten Delaware’s ban, if a challenge was brought in court. It was enacted in 2022 after mass shootings at an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, and at a supermarket in Buffalo, N.Y.

Virginia’s law was enacted this year, and the Trump administration was among those challenging it at the federal or state level. A judge paused the legal challenges, and the law cannot take effect before the Supreme Court rules.

Note: In Hawaii, high-capacity magazines are only restricted for assault pistols.

Sources: Everytown Research & Policy and Giffords Law Center.

Daniel Wood/The New York Times

Assault weapons are defined by features that make a gun easier for a person to carry and sustain fire at a rapid clip — the more quickly someone can fire off bullets, the more deadly the weapon.

That’s why states that have restricted assault weapons also limit high-capacity magazines, which store and feed ammunition to the firearm. A few states that do not prohibit assault weapons instead restrict the high-capacity magazines, which allow an assailant to fire more than 10 to 20 bullets before needing to pause to reload.

The Supreme Court has not indicated whether it will weigh in on the legality of restricting high-capacity magazines.

Four states have passed laws prohibiting Glocks or Glock-style pistols, but California is the only state where the law has gone into effect.

Unlike restrictions on assault weapons, these prohibitions are new, brought on by the rise of switches, an illegal gun accessory that allows a semiautomatic handgun to fire at the rate of a machine gun.

Switches are small and often made of plastic, making them easy and cheap to manufacture. To curb their spread, some states have restricted the model of handgun that is easily modified by a switch.

The Trump administration has already sued California over its restrictions, arguing that “perfectly legal and safe firearms” should not be banned simply because they can be converted into illegal firearms.

The Supreme Court is expected to weigh the constitutionality of assault weapons bans in part by a standard that weighs how commonly they are used. Depending on how the justices rule, their ruling could affect how judges evaluate challenges to bans on the Glock, an Austrian-made pistol that has become a household name.

item.title: Sherrod Brown Tries a New Retort to Criticism on Transgender Issues
item.description:
Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Ohio, has spent more than $200,000 on a 30-second advertisement responding to attacks from his opponent and an Elon Musk-backed PAC regarding transgender issues, according to AdImpact.

Here’s a look at the ad, its accuracy and its major takeaway.

The ad opens with voters identified as Beth and Warren in Johnstown, Ohio, an agricultural hub just south of Columbus that has historically leaned Republican.

Warren speaks first, looking directly at the camera, and says, “Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown.”

The ad then pans to a voter in Granville, a Democratic island in a conservative part of the state, who says, “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?”

As another voter speaks, a text overlay on an image of a dark, empty hospital hallway reads: “IN OHIO IT’S ILLEGAL TO PERFORM TRANSGENDER SURGERIES ON CHILDREN.”

A series of voters in different parts of the state then denounce Senator Jon Husted, Mr. Brown’s Republican opponent, accusing him of voting to increase the cost of groceries, kicking hundreds of thousands of Ohioans off health care, writing a law letting utility companies “jack up our electric bills,” and failing to address the cost of gas.

The ad ends with Beth in Johnstown, who faces the camera and says “John Husted, why don’t you start working for us?”

Mr. Brown is in a high-stakes race against Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat of JD Vance when he left to become vice president. Mr. Brown has faced a torrent of negative advertising focusing on transgender issues.

“Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown. With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about. In Ohio, it’s against the law to perform transgender surgeries on kids. That’s right, it’s illegal. Jon Husted, why’d you vote to increase the cost of groceries? To do nothing about the cost of gas. You kicked 490,000 Ohioans off their health care. And Jon Husted wrote the law on letting utility companies jack up our electric bills. Jon Husted, why don’t you start working for us? I’m Sherrod Brown and I approve this message.”

The advertisement is correct that an Ohio law passed in 2024, over the Republican governor’s veto, forbids doctors from prescribing medications that assist minors seeking gender transitions. The law also restricts transgender girls and women from competing in girls and women’s sports.

The law is being challenged before the state Supreme Court, which is made up of six Republican justices and one Democrat.

It is misleading to say that Mr. Husted voted to “increase the cost of groceries,” because there was not a specific vote on that issue in the Senate. But he has supported sweeping tariffs and the war with Iran, among other policies, that have contributed to the rising prices, including of groceries and gas.

Mr. Husted also voted for President Trump’s signature domestic policy bill, which included significant cuts to Medicaid and Medicare. The Joint Economic Committee, a bipartisan group, estimated that more that 489,815 Ohioans would lose health insurance as a result of the cuts.

The claim that Mr. Husted wrote a law that allowed utility companies to raise prices is accurate and complicated. Mr. Husted, then a lieutenant governor, was highly involved in passing a 2019 energy law that later became the center of a massive bribery scheme that landed another lawmaker, the former speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, in prison.

The law allowed utility companies to add extra fees and surcharges to electricity bills as a bailout for two struggling nuclear power plants. Mr. Husted has denied any knowledge of wrongdoing in the high-profile scandal.

This spot represents a new response to the Republican Party’s effort to use transgender issues to paint Democrats as radical and unelectable, regardless of their specific stances, which tend to be more nuanced than portrayed by their opponents.

Instead of engaging on the topic, Mr. Brown’s campaign is seeking to dismiss it as irrelevant, and a distraction from the economic issues that they hope will drive voters to the polls.

item.title: Man Charged in Boy’s Disappearance After 33 Years
item.description:
When 10-year-old George Burdynski Jr. hopped on his bike on May 24, 1993, near his Maryland home, it was the last time his family saw him.

The disappearance of George, who was also known as Junior, shocked Prince George’s County in Maryland and prompted a large manhunt by law enforcement, including the F.B.I. Volunteers also joined the search.

But the case languished for more than 33 years.

Now, investigators say they have arrested a 61-year-old man, Joseph Lynch, who has been charged with second-degree murder, rape and other sexual abuse charges in connection with George’s disappearance.

Another person, a 47-year-old man, whom Mr. Lynch also sexually assaulted, admitted to beating George to death, the authorities said.

That unidentified man has not been charged, the Prince George’s County Police Department said. The county state attorney’s office would not comment on Friday.

“We held onto hope for 33 years,” said Virginia Burdynski, George’s sister, at a news conference on Thursday. “This is not what we prayed for.”

Mr. Lynch appeared in court on Friday and was being held without bail, according to court records. A lawyer representing him could not immediately be reached.

Investigators got a break in the case after a witness, the 47-year-old man, stepped forward in June and said he was with George and Mr. Lynch at the time of the boy’s disappearance.

The witness, who was 13 in 1993, lived in George’s neighborhood.

Mr. Lynch physically and sexually assaulted the witness on the day that George disappeared, according to a statement of charges.

On that same day, Mr. Lynch forced the witness to sexually assault George while Mr. Lynch watched, the statement said.

Mr. Lynch is accused of establishing control over the witness, compelling his participation and standing in a doorway to prevent the witness from leaving, the statement said.

“The witness stated that immediately thereafter, he became extremely angry because of the physical and sexual abuse he had endured from the suspect earlier that morning,” the statement of charges said.

The witness told investigators he could not direct his anger toward Mr. Lynch and instead targeted George, who was younger and smaller, the statement said.

“The witness admitted repeatedly punching and kicking the victim until the victim stopped moving,” the statement said. “The witness recalled observing blood coming from the victim’s head and believed that the victim was dead or had been fatally injured.”

Mr. Lynch retrieved a knife, tarp and rope and rolled George inside, the statement said.

Mr. Lynch and the witness carried George’s body to a location in Prince George’s County and disposed of him, the statement said.

George’s body has never been found.

“Taken together, the suspect’s actions before, during and immediately after the offenses establish that he was an active participant in the continuous course of criminal conduct that resulted in the victim’s death,” the statement.

Mr. Lynch had been previously convicted in 1994 of two sex offenses involving minors, said Chief George R. Nader of the Prince George’s County Police Department.

George was not identified as a victim in that case, the chief said.

Mr. Lynch was sentenced to 20 years in prison and was released in 2006, Chief Nader said.

The chief said he believed there were other victims.

“They have a voice,” he said. “We want to hear from them.”

The testimony of the witness who confessed to killing George may be central to the prosecution’s case, especially if little evidence has survived, said Max Frizalone, a criminal defense lawyer based in Maryland who is not involved in the case.

If the witness invokes his Fifth Amendment right to refuse to incriminate himself by testifying, that could put the prosecution’s case in jeopardy, he said.

Prosecutors may have sought immunity for the witness, Mr. Frizalone said.

“A prosecutor who concluded that the adult directed the killing and that the child acted under his domination would have a coherent reason both to charge Lynch with murder and to use the witness as a witness rather than a defendant,” he said.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Newsom Signs Bills Meant to Prevent Trump’s Interference in Midterms
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation on Saturday that is meant to prevent interference in California’s midterm elections in response to efforts by President Trump and other Republicans to restrict voting participation.

Mr. Newsom and fellow Democrats in the State Legislature crafted the bills to broadly combat involvement by the Trump administration, without knowing specifically whether or how the federal government might engage in California’s elections. The state relies heavily on mail ballots, and Mr. Trump has taken particular aim at that form of voting.

One bill prohibits the seizure of ballots, election records or voting technology before an election is certified. Another makes it a felony for people in positions of authority to direct their workers to interfere with the delivery of a mail ballot or its return to election officials.

Mr. Newsom signed a package of 13 bills, including a measure that prohibits arrests within 200 feet of a polling place on Election Day, with exceptions for acts related to disrupting the election or crimes against people or property. Democrats have feared that the Trump administration could send federal agents to polling places in immigrant communities.

Mr. Trump, who has voted by mail twice this year, has claimed that absentee voting is rife with fraud. He and his administration said in July, without evidence, that California and three other states had allowed about 278,000 noncitizens to vote in federal elections.

California’s Democratic leaders said they were responding to a spate of unusual challenges from Mr. Trump, and local officials aligned with him. Mr. Newsom signed the bills in Los Angeles at the Japanese American National Museum, where Border Patrol agents showed up outside a rally the governor held last summer.

Mr. Trump signed an executive order in March that sought to restrict the use of mail ballots. And earlier this year, Chad Bianco, the Republican sheriff in Riverside County, seized more than 650,000 ballots that voters had cast last year because he said he was investigating a discrepancy in the count. California challenged both actions in court. The Supreme Court on Monday sided with California and other Democratic-led states by blocking Mr. Trump’s plan to restrict voting by mail.

The new state laws add small but meaningful protections to California’s ability to prevent outside involvement in its ballot process, said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University who worked on voting rights for the Biden administration.

“There’s a vigilante mood afoot,” Mr. Levitt said. “This acts as a little bit of a deterrent for people who are cosplaying election officials.”

Shannon Grove, a Republican state senator who voted against the bills, said she believed one of the laws would allow criminal charges against U.S. Postal Service workers who handle ballots as a routine part of their job. Under that bill, it would be a misdemeanor for anyone in charge of a mail ballot to interfere with delivering it to a voter.

“This is about the postal workers, and that’s pretty bold,” she said.

In a brief interview last month, Mr. Newsom said the legislation wasn’t aimed at prosecuting postal workers who are doing their jobs properly.

The bills are targeted at those “carrying out illegal activity or illegal orders and directives,” Mr. Newsom said. “With these enhanced sanctions, if you break the law we’re going to hold you accountable, and it doesn’t matter who you are.”

Among the other bills that Mr. Newsom signed are two that took aim at “deepfake” ads generated by A.I. that mimic a politician’s voice or appearance to deceive voters.

In 2024, voters in New Hampshire received a voice message that was made to sound like President Joseph R. Biden Jr. urging them not to vote. That same year, an online ad imitated the voice of Vice President Kamala Harris saying Mr. Biden was senile.

California passed legislation cracking down on deepfake political ads that year, but it was later blocked by courts for violating free speech. The new legislation takes a narrower approach meant to strengthen it against constitutional challenges.

Mr. Newsom also signed a bill that could accelerate California’s notoriously slow process for counting votes.

It calls for election officials to tell people how to vote early, which reduces the glut of envelopes that arrive on Election Day. It also requires informing voters that they can submit mail ballots at a polling place. Doing so allows election officials to count ballots faster by eliminating the envelopes that are cumbersome to process.

Most election-related bills relied on Democratic support to pass, but the legislation to encourage early voting and in-person submission of ballots had sweeping bipartisan support.

Rick Hasen, an election law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said he was skeptical that California would be successful in stopping officials from the U.S. Department of Justice if they tried to collect ballots during an election, a scenario that has not occurred in modern times.

But, he said, the laws could be enforced against state and local officials. The state has already sued Mr. Bianco, and the parties in that case are awaiting a decision from the California Supreme Court.
